# Existence of a Minimal Uncountable Well-Ordered Set (without the Axiom of Choice)

**Theorem.** There exists an uncountable well-ordered set $(\Omega,\preceq)$ such that every initial
segment of $\Omega$ is countable. The proof below uses only the axioms of ZF (Extensionality,
Pairing, Union, Power Set, Separation, Replacement, Infinity); the Axiom of Choice is never invoked.

## 0. Conventions

A *well-ordered set* is a pair $(S,\le)$ where $\le$ is a total (linear) ordering of $S$ such that
**every nonempty** subset of $S$ has a least element. We write $x<y$ for $x\le y\wedge x\ne y$.

For $a\in S$ the *initial segment determined by $a$* is
$$S_a \;=\; \{x\in S : x<a\},$$
ordered by the restriction of $\le$; we write $\le_a$ for that restriction. These are exactly the
*proper* initial segments in the sense of the statement. (Remark 7.1 below shows the theorem also
holds verbatim under the alternative convention in which an initial segment means an arbitrary
proper down-closed subset.)

A subset of a well-ordered set, with the induced ordering, is again well-ordered: it is totally
ordered, and each of its nonempty subsets is a nonempty subset of $S$ and so has a least element,
which lies in the subset. In particular each $(S_a,\le_a)$ is well-ordered.

An *order isomorphism* $f\colon (S,\le)\to(T,\sqsubseteq)$ is a bijection with
$x\le y \iff f(x)\sqsubseteq f(y)$; we write $(S,\le)\cong(T,\sqsubseteq)$, or $S\cong T$ when the
orderings are clear. Note that an order isomorphism is strictly increasing, and that identities,
inverses and composites of order isomorphisms are order isomorphisms, so $\cong$ is an equivalence
relation wherever it is applied below.

A set $X$ is *countable* iff there is an injection $X\to\mathbb N$ (so finite sets count as
countable), and *uncountable* otherwise. $\mathbb N$ denotes the set of natural numbers.

Throughout, phrases such as "fix an element of the nonempty set $X$" are single applications of
existential instantiation, not applications of the Axiom of Choice: at no point is a choice function
on an infinite family required.

## 1. Basic lemmas on well-ordered sets

**Lemma 1.** *Let $(S,\le)$ be well-ordered and let $f\colon S\to S$ be strictly increasing (i.e.
$x<y\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)$). Then $a\le f(a)$ for every $a\in S$.*

*Proof.* Put $T=\{a\in S: f(a)<a\}$, a subset of $S$ by Separation. Suppose, for contradiction, that
$T\ne\varnothing$. Only under this assumption may we apply the well-ordering: since $T$ is a
*nonempty* subset of $S$, it has a least element $t$. By definition of $T$ we have $s:=f(t)<t$.
Applying the strictly increasing map $f$ to $s<t$ gives $f(s)<f(t)=s$, so $s\in T$; but $s<t$
contradicts the minimality of $t$ in $T$. Hence $T=\varnothing$, i.e. no $a$ satisfies $f(a)<a$.
Since $\le$ is total, $a\le f(a)$ for every $a\in S$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2 (no self-embedding onto an initial segment).** *A well-ordered set $(S,\le)$ is not order
isomorphic to any of its initial segments $(S_a,\le_a)$.*

*Proof.* Suppose $f\colon S\to S_a$ were an order isomorphism for some $a\in S$. Since $S_a\subseteq
S$ and the ordering on $S_a$ is the restriction of $\le$, the map $f$, viewed as a map $S\to S$, is
strictly increasing. Lemma 1 gives $a\le f(a)$. But $f(a)\in S_a$ means $f(a)<a$, a contradiction.
$\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3 (uniqueness of isomorphisms).** *If $f,g\colon (S,\le)\to(T,\sqsubseteq)$ are order
isomorphisms of well-ordered sets, then $f=g$.*

*Proof.* $g^{-1}\circ f\colon S\to S$ is strictly increasing, so by Lemma 1, $a\le g^{-1}(f(a))$ for
all $a$, and applying the increasing map $g$ gives $g(a)\sqsubseteq f(a)$. Exchanging the roles of
$f$ and $g$ gives $f(a)\sqsubseteq g(a)$. By antisymmetry $f(a)=g(a)$ for all $a$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 4 (isomorphisms match initial segments exactly).** *Let $f\colon (S,\le)\to(T,\sqsubseteq)$
be an order isomorphism of well-ordered sets and let $a\in S$. Then*
$$f[S_a]\;=\;T_{f(a)},$$
*and the restriction $f\restriction S_a\colon (S_a,\le_a)\to (T_{f(a)},\sqsubseteq_{f(a)})$ is an
order isomorphism.*

*Proof.* We prove the two inclusions separately; neither is assumed.

$\subseteq$: if $x\in S_a$ then $x<a$, so $f(x)\sqsubset f(a)$ because $f$ is strictly increasing;
thus $f(x)\in T_{f(a)}$.

$\supseteq$: let $y\in T_{f(a)}$, so $y\sqsubset f(a)$. Since $f$ is **surjective** onto $T$, there
is $x\in S$ with $f(x)=y$. Since $\le$ is total, either $x<a$ or $a\le x$. If $a\le x$ then
$f(a)\sqsubseteq f(x)=y$, contradicting $y\sqsubset f(a)$. Hence $x<a$, i.e. $x\in S_a$ and
$y=f(x)\in f[S_a]$.

Consequently $f\restriction S_a$ is a bijection of $S_a$ onto $T_{f(a)}$; it is injective as a
restriction of an injection, and it preserves and reflects the orderings because $f$ does and the
orderings on $S_a,T_{f(a)}$ are the restricted ones. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 5 (distinct initial segments are non-isomorphic).** *Let $(S,\le)$ be well-ordered and
$a,b\in S$ with $a\ne b$. Then $(S_a,\le_a)\not\cong(S_b,\le_b)$.*

*Proof.* By totality we may assume $a<b$ (otherwise swap the names). Then $a\in S_b$, and
$$(S_b)_a=\{x\in S: x<b \text{ and } x<a\}=\{x\in S: x<a\}=S_a,$$
the second equality because $x<a<b$ forces $x<b$ by transitivity. So $S_a$ is an initial segment of
the well-ordered set $S_b$, and Lemma 2 applied to $(S_b,\le_b)$ gives $S_b\not\cong S_a$.
$\blacksquare$

**Lemma 6 (trichotomy; choice-free).** *Let $(S,\le)$ and $(T,\sqsubseteq)$ be well-ordered sets.
Then exactly one of the following holds:*

1. $S\cong T$;
2. $S\cong T_b$ for a (necessarily unique) $b\in T$;
3. $S_a\cong T$ for a (necessarily unique) $a\in S$.

*Proof.* By Separation inside $S\times T$ define
$$h=\{(x,y)\in S\times T:\ (S_x,\le_x)\cong (T_y,\sqsubseteq_y)\}.$$

*(a) $h$ is an injective function.* If $(x,y),(x,y')\in h$ then $T_y\cong S_x\cong T_{y'}$, so
$y=y'$ by Lemma 5 applied in $T$. If $(x,y),(x',y)\in h$ then $S_x\cong T_y\cong S_{x'}$, so $x=x'$
by Lemma 5 applied in $S$.

Write $D=\operatorname{dom}h$ and $E=\operatorname{ran}h$.

*(b) $D$ is down-closed, $h$ is strictly increasing, and $E$ is down-closed.* Let $x\in D$ and let
$f\colon S_x\to T_{h(x)}$ be an order isomorphism. Let $x'<x$, so $x'\in S_x$. Inside the
well-ordered set $S_x$ we have $(S_x)_{x'}=S_{x'}$ (as in Lemma 5, since $x'<x$), and inside
$T_{h(x)}$ we have $(T_{h(x)})_{z}=T_{z}$ for every $z\in T_{h(x)}$ (same computation, since
$z\sqsubset h(x)$). Applying Lemma 4 to the isomorphism $f$ and the point $x'\in S_x$ yields
$$S_{x'}=(S_x)_{x'}\ \cong\ (T_{h(x)})_{f(x')}=T_{f(x')} .$$
Hence $x'\in D$ and $h(x')=f(x')$ (using (a)). This shows $D$ is down-closed. Moreover
$f(x')\in T_{h(x)}$ means $h(x')=f(x')\sqsubset h(x)$, so $h$ is strictly increasing on $D$; being
an injective, strictly increasing map between totally ordered sets, $h\colon D\to E$ both preserves
and reflects the orderings, hence is an order isomorphism of $(D,\le)$ onto $(E,\sqsubseteq)$. For
$E$: let $y\sqsubset h(x)$ with $x\in D$. By Lemma 4, $T_{h(x)}=f[S_x]$ **exactly**, so there is
$x'\in S_x$ with $f(x')=y$; by the previous sentence $x'\in D$ and $h(x')=f(x')=y$, so $y\in E$.

*(c) $D=S$ or $E=T$.* Suppose not, i.e. $D\ne S$ and $E\ne T$. Since $D\subseteq S$ and $E\subseteq
T$, the sets $S\setminus D$ and $T\setminus E$ are then both **nonempty**, and only now do we invoke
the well-orderings: let $a$ be the least element of $S\setminus D$ and $b$ the least element of
$T\setminus E$. Then $D=S_a$: if $x<a$ then $x\notin S\setminus D$ by minimality of $a$, so $x\in
D$; conversely if $x\in D$ then $x\ne a$ (as $a\notin D$) and not $a<x$ (else $a\in D$ by
down-closedness of $D$), so $x<a$ by totality. Symmetrically $E=T_b$. But then $h\colon S_a\to T_b$
is an order isomorphism by (b), so $(a,b)\in h$ by the definition of $h$, i.e. $a\in D=S_a$, i.e.
$a<a$ — a contradiction. Hence $D=S$ or $E=T$.

*(d) At least one of 1.–3. holds.* If $D=S$ and $E=T$, then $h$ witnesses $S\cong T$, case 1. If
$D=S$ and $E\ne T$, then by the argument in (c) applied to $T$ alone, $E=T_b$ where $b$ is the least
element of the nonempty set $T\setminus E$; then $h$ witnesses $S\cong T_b$, case 2. If $D\ne S$ and
$E=T$, then likewise $D=S_a$ and $h$ witnesses $S_a\cong T$, case 3.

*(e) At most one of 1.–3. holds, and the witnesses are unique.* If 1 and 2 both held, then
$T\cong S\cong T_b$, contradicting Lemma 2 in $T$. If 1 and 3 both held, then $S\cong T\cong S_a$,
contradicting Lemma 2 in $S$. If 2 and 3 both held, take isomorphisms $u\colon S\to T_b$ and
$g\colon T\to S_a$. Since $b\in T$, Lemma 4 applied to $g$ gives
$T_b\cong (S_a)_{g(b)}=S_{g(b)}$ (the last equality because $g(b)\in S_a$, so $g(b)<a$). Hence
$S\cong T_b\cong S_{g(b)}$, contradicting Lemma 2 in $S$. Uniqueness of $b$ in case 2 follows from
Lemma 5 in $T$ (if $S\cong T_b$ and $S\cong T_{b'}$ then $T_b\cong T_{b'}$, so $b=b'$), and
uniqueness of $a$ in case 3 from Lemma 5 in $S$. $\blacksquare$

## 2. The set $\Omega$

By the Power Set and Separation axioms, the following is a set:
$$\mathcal W=\bigl\{(A,R)\in\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\times\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times\mathbb N)\ :\
R\subseteq A\times A\ \text{and}\ R\ \text{is a well-ordering of}\ A\bigr\}.$$
(The condition "$R$ is a well-ordering of $A$" is a formula with parameters $A,R$, so Separation
applies.) Note $(\varnothing,\varnothing)\in\mathcal W$, so $\mathcal W\ne\varnothing$.

For $(B,S)\in\mathcal W$ and $b\in B$ we write
$$B_b=\{x\in B: (x,b)\in S,\ x\ne b\},\qquad S_b=S\cap(B_b\times B_b),$$
so that $(B_b,S_b)$ is the initial segment of $(B,S)$ determined by $b$. Since $B_b\subseteq
B\subseteq\mathbb N$ and a subset of a well-ordered set is well-ordered by the restricted ordering,
we have $(B_b,S_b)\in\mathcal W$.

Order isomorphism $\cong$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathcal W$. Let
$$\Omega=\mathcal W/{\cong}$$
be the set of its equivalence classes (a subset of $\mathcal P(\mathcal W)$, obtained by Separation,
or by Replacement applied to $\mathcal W$); write $[A,R]$ for the class of $(A,R)$. Since
$\mathcal W\ne\varnothing$, also $\Omega\ne\varnothing$.

**Definition.** For $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ put $\alpha\preceq\beta$ iff for some (equivalently, as
shown next, for all) representatives $(A,R)\in\alpha$ and $(B,S)\in\beta$:
$$(A,R)\cong(B,S)\quad\text{or}\quad (A,R)\cong(B_b,S_b)\ \text{for some } b\in B .$$

**Lemma 7 ($\preceq$ is well defined).** *The truth of the displayed condition does not depend on
the representatives chosen.*

*Proof.* Let $(A,R)\cong(A',R')$ and $(B,S)\cong(B',S')$, and fix an order isomorphism $g\colon
B\to B'$. If $(A,R)\cong(B,S)$ then $(A',R')\cong(A,R)\cong(B,S)\cong(B',S')$. If
$(A,R)\cong(B_b,S_b)$ for some $b\in B$, then Lemma 4 gives $(B_b,S_b)\cong(B'_{g(b)},S'_{g(b)})$
with $g(b)\in B'$, whence $(A',R')\cong(B'_{g(b)},S'_{g(b)})$. The converse directions follow by
symmetry. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 8.** *$(\Omega,\preceq)$ is a totally ordered set.*

*Proof.* *Reflexivity* is clear (take the first alternative). *Antisymmetry:* suppose
$[A,R]\preceq[B,S]$, $[B,S]\preceq[A,R]$ and $[A,R]\ne[B,S]$. Then $(A,R)\not\cong(B,S)$, so the
second alternative must hold both ways: $A\cong B_b$ and $B\cong A_a$ for some $b\in B,a\in A$. That
is, cases 2 and 3 of Lemma 6 hold simultaneously, which Lemma 6(e) forbids. Hence $[A,R]=[B,S]$.
*Transitivity:* let $[A,R]\preceq[B,S]\preceq[C,U]$. If $(B,S)\cong(C,U)$, transport the first
relation along this isomorphism exactly as in Lemma 7 to get $[A,R]\preceq[C,U]$. If $(A,R)\cong
(B,S)$, then $[A,R]=[B,S]\preceq[C,U]$. In the remaining case $A\cong B_b$ and $B\cong C_c$ for some
$b\in B$, $c\in C$; letting $g\colon B\to C_c$ be an isomorphism, Lemma 4 gives
$B_b\cong (C_c)_{g(b)}=C_{g(b)}$ (using $g(b)\in C_c$, i.e. $g(b)<_U c$), hence $A\cong C_{g(b)}$
and $[A,R]\preceq[C,U]$. *Totality:* by Lemma 6 one of its three cases holds for $(A,R),(B,S)$,
giving respectively $[A,R]=[B,S]$, $[A,R]\preceq[B,S]$, or $[B,S]\preceq[A,R]$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 9 (description of strict predecessors).** *Let $(B,S)\in\mathcal W$ and $\gamma\in\Omega$.
Then $\gamma\prec[B,S]$ (i.e. $\gamma\preceq[B,S]$ and $\gamma\ne[B,S]$) if and only if
$\gamma=[B_b,S_b]$ for some $b\in B$.*

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) $\gamma\preceq[B,S]$ with $\gamma\ne[B,S]$ rules out the first alternative
in the definition, leaving $\gamma=[B_b,S_b]$ for some $b\in B$. ($\Leftarrow$) $[B_b,S_b]\preceq
[B,S]$ holds by definition, and $[B_b,S_b]\ne[B,S]$ since $(B,S)\not\cong(B_b,S_b)$ by Lemma 2.
$\blacksquare$

**Proposition 10.** *$(\Omega,\preceq)$ is a well-ordered set.*

*Proof.* By Lemma 8, $\preceq$ is a total ordering. Let $C\subseteq\Omega$ be **nonempty**. Because
$C\ne\varnothing$ we may fix one element $\gamma_0\in C$, and because the equivalence class
$\gamma_0$ is itself nonempty we may fix one representative $(B,S)\in\mathcal W$ with
$\gamma_0=[B,S]$. (Two single existential instantiations; no choice function is formed.) By
Separation put
$$D=\{b\in B:\ [B_b,S_b]\in C\}\subseteq B .$$

*Case 1: $D=\varnothing$.* We claim $\gamma_0$ is the least element of $C$. Let $\gamma\in C$. By
totality, $\gamma\preceq\gamma_0$ or $\gamma_0\preceq\gamma$. In the first case, if
$\gamma\ne\gamma_0$ then Lemma 9 gives $\gamma=[B_b,S_b]$ for some $b\in B$, so $b\in D$,
contradicting $D=\varnothing$; hence $\gamma=\gamma_0$. Either way $\gamma_0\preceq\gamma$. As
$\gamma_0\in C$, it is the least element of $C$.

*Case 2: $D\ne\varnothing$.* Only now, $D$ being a **nonempty** subset of the well-ordered set
$(B,S)$, may we take its $S$-least element $b_0$. Put $\mu=[B_{b_0},S_{b_0}]$; then $\mu\in C$ by
the definition of $D$. Let $\gamma\in C$. By totality, $\mu\preceq\gamma$ or $\gamma\preceq\mu$.
Suppose $\gamma\preceq\mu$ and $\gamma\ne\mu$. By Lemma 9 applied to $(B_{b_0},S_{b_0})$, there is
$x\in B_{b_0}$ with $\gamma=[(B_{b_0})_x,(S_{b_0})_x]$. Since $x<_S b_0$, exactly as in Lemma 5 we
have $(B_{b_0})_x=B_x$ and hence $(S_{b_0})_x=S_x$, so $\gamma=[B_x,S_x]$ with $x\in B$; thus $x\in
D$ and $x<_S b_0$, contradicting the $S$-minimality of $b_0$ in $D$. Therefore $\mu\preceq\gamma$
for all $\gamma\in C$, and $\mu$ is the least element of $C$.

In both cases $C$ has a least element, so $(\Omega,\preceq)$ is well-ordered. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Every initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable

**Proposition 11.** *Let $\omega=[A,R]\in\Omega$. Then the map*
$$\Phi\colon A\to\Omega,\qquad \Phi(a)=[A_a,R_a]$$
*is an order isomorphism of $(A,R)$ onto the initial segment $(\Omega_\omega,\preceq_\omega)$. In
particular $\Omega_\omega$ is countable.*

*Proof.* $\Phi$ is a well-defined function on $A$ (its value is determined by $a$), and:

*Range.* For $a\in A$, Lemma 9 gives $[A_a,R_a]\prec[A,R]=\omega$, so $\Phi(a)\in\Omega_\omega$.

*Surjectivity onto $\Omega_\omega$.* If $\gamma\in\Omega_\omega$, i.e. $\gamma\prec\omega$, then by
Lemma 9 $\gamma=[A_a,R_a]=\Phi(a)$ for some $a\in A$.

*Injectivity.* If $a\ne a'$ in $A$, then $(A_a,R_a)\not\cong(A_{a'},R_{a'})$ by Lemma 5, so
$\Phi(a)\ne\Phi(a')$.

*Order preservation.* Let $a<_R a'$. Then, as in Lemma 5, $A_a=(A_{a'})_a$ and $R_a=(R_{a'})_a$, so
$(A_a,R_a)$ is an initial segment of $(A_{a'},R_{a'})$ and Lemma 9 yields $\Phi(a)\prec\Phi(a')$.
Conversely, if $\Phi(a)\prec\Phi(a')$ then $a\ne a'$ (as $\Phi$ is a function) and $a'<_R a$ is
impossible (it would give $\Phi(a')\prec\Phi(a)$, contradicting antisymmetry), so $a<_R a'$ by
totality of $R$.

Thus $\Phi$ is an order isomorphism onto $\Omega_\omega$. Finally, $\Phi^{-1}\colon
\Omega_\omega\to A$ is a bijection and $A\subseteq\mathbb N$, so the composite of $\Phi^{-1}$ with
the inclusion $A\hookrightarrow\mathbb N$ is an injection $\Omega_\omega\to\mathbb N$. Hence
$\Omega_\omega$ is countable. $\blacksquare$

## 4. $\Omega$ is uncountable

**Proposition 12.** *$\Omega$ is uncountable.*

*Proof.* Suppose, for contradiction, that $\Omega$ is countable, and fix an injection
$j\colon\Omega\to\mathbb N$. Put
$$A=j[\Omega]\subseteq\mathbb N,\qquad R=\{(j(\alpha),j(\beta)) : \alpha,\beta\in\Omega,\
\alpha\preceq\beta\}\subseteq A\times A .$$
Both are sets by Replacement and Separation.

*$j$ is an order isomorphism $(\Omega,\preceq)\to(A,R)$.* It is a bijection onto $A$ by construction
and injectivity. If $\alpha\preceq\beta$ then $(j(\alpha),j(\beta))\in R$ by definition. Conversely,
if $(j(\alpha),j(\beta))\in R$ then $j(\alpha)=j(\alpha')$, $j(\beta)=j(\beta')$ for some
$\alpha'\preceq\beta'$; injectivity of $j$ gives $\alpha=\alpha'$ and $\beta=\beta'$, so
$\alpha\preceq\beta$.

*$(A,R)\in\mathcal W$.* Transporting along the bijection $j$: $R$ is reflexive, antisymmetric,
transitive and total on $A$ because $\preceq$ is on $\Omega$; and if $\varnothing\ne X\subseteq A$,
then $j^{-1}[X]$ is a nonempty subset of $\Omega$, which by Proposition 10 has a $\preceq$-least
element $\alpha$, and then $j(\alpha)$ is the $R$-least element of $X$. So $R$ is a well-ordering of
the set $A\subseteq\mathbb N$, i.e. $(A,R)\in\mathcal W$.

Hence $\omega^{*}:=[A,R]\in\Omega$. By Proposition 11 applied to $\omega^{*}$,
$$(\Omega_{\omega^{*}},\preceq_{\omega^{*}})\ \cong\ (A,R)\ \cong\ (\Omega,\preceq),$$
the last isomorphism being $j^{-1}$. So the well-ordered set $(\Omega,\preceq)$ (well-ordered by
Proposition 10) is order isomorphic to its own initial segment $\Omega_{\omega^{*}}$, contradicting
Lemma 2.

Therefore no injection $\Omega\to\mathbb N$ exists, i.e. $\Omega$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Conclusion

By Proposition 10, $(\Omega,\preceq)$ is a well-ordered set; by Proposition 12 it is uncountable; and
by Proposition 11 every initial segment $\Omega_\omega$ ($\omega\in\Omega$) is countable. Hence
$(\Omega,\preceq)$ is a minimal uncountable well-ordered set, and such a set exists. $\blacksquare$

## 6. Remark on the use of the Axiom of Choice

Every object above was defined explicitly: $\mathcal W$ by Separation from
$\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\times\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times\mathbb N)$; $\Omega$ as a quotient by an
explicitly defined equivalence relation; $\preceq$, $h$, $D$, $\Phi$, $A$, $R$ by explicit formulas.
The only "choices" made are finitely many single existential instantiations (an element $\gamma_0$ of
a nonempty set $C$, a representative of the nonempty class $\gamma_0$, an isomorphism between two
sets already known to be isomorphic — and by Lemma 3 such an isomorphism is in fact unique, so even
this is canonical). No choice function on an infinite family is ever formed, so the proof is carried
out entirely in ZF.

## 7. Remarks

**7.1 (Other convention for "initial segment").** Some texts call a subset $I\subseteq S$ an initial
segment when it is down-closed ($y\in I$ and $x<y$ imply $x\in I$) and proper. In a well-ordered set
these are exactly the sets $S_a$: the argument in Lemma 6(c) shows that if $I\subsetneq S$ is
down-closed, then $S\setminus I$ is nonempty, so it has a least element $a$, and $I=S_a$. Hence
Proposition 11 already covers all initial segments in that sense too, and the theorem holds under
either convention.

**7.2 (Uniqueness up to isomorphism).** Although not asserted by the theorem, Lemma 6 shows any two
minimal uncountable well-ordered sets are order isomorphic: if $\Omega,\Omega'$ are two such and,
say, $\Omega\cong\Omega'_{b}$ for some $b\in\Omega'$, then $\Omega$ would be countable, a
contradiction; symmetrically for the third case; so case 1 of Lemma 6 must hold.
